Subject: Post-call: Performance SLO & next steps

Thanks again for taking the time today — great conversation. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we have a shared record: 

Summary of requirements (from our call)
- Latency targets: p50 <= 150ms, p95 <= 300ms for single-turn generation (average prompt lengths ~300-500 tokens).
- Streaming: partial-token streaming is required for UI responsiveness; goal is first-chunk delivered <= 50ms after generation starts.
- Throughput/concurrency: baseline 50 QPS sustained, burst to 150 QPS; typical concurrency during peak 120 simultaneous user flows.
- Sequence lengths: 1k tokens max; typical average 400 tokens.
- Determinism: non-deterministic acceptable, but we need stable quality across runs; please flag strict sampling constraints if present.

Requested deliverables from Redwood
- Benchmark methodology (prompt sets, harness, measurement definitions) that we can review for reproducibility.
- A proposed test plan and timeline for running benchmarks in Redwood Hosted/Dedicated.
- Any hardware assumptions (GPU type, batch sizing, quantization profile) and how they map to the performance numbers.

Attachments: I’m attaching the SLO/req doc you shared on the call (fineedge_slo_requirements.pdf).

Next steps:
1) Kyle/Sana: confirm the bullets above and add anything missing (esp. streaming chunk size expectations and any max acceptable tail latency p99).
2) We'll share a benchmark plan (Marcus) and a reproducible harness for you to review.
3) Agree on target date for a joint benchmark run (we suggested next week on the call).

Thanks — I’ll coordinate schedules once we confirm.

Best,

Thanks Marissa — that matches our notes. A few clarifications / additions: 
- Streaming: our UI consumes partial tokens in ~64-token chunks; we'd like the first chunk to be visible in the client within 50ms of generation start and subsequent chunks at steady cadence. If you have any authoritative measurement approach for chunk-level latency, please include it.
- Tail: p99 should ideally be <= 500ms but we understand p99 is much harder at scale — we can tolerate occasional spikes if documented.
- Concurrency: apologies — corrective number: sustained 75 QPS, burst up to 200 QPS for short periods (1-2 mins). Peak simultaneous sessions ~150.
- Prompt diversity: we have 3 categories — short queries (<=64 tokens), multi-turn context (avg 400 tokens), and long-form summarization (700-1k tokens). We can provide a representative prompt set but need the benchmark harness to allow us to drop in our prompts.

We’d like Redwood to run the initial benchmark on a Dedicated node that approximates our planned production config (single A100-class GPU to start) and share raw logs (latency histograms, traces) so our infra team can vet the assumptions. Can you confirm whether Redwood can provide that level of detail and if any NDA is needed before we share the full prompt set?

–Kyle

Subject: RE: Post-call: Performance SLO & next steps — proposed benchmark methodology

Hi Kyle / Sana —

Thanks for the clarifications. I’m Marcus (serving/runtime lead) — copying a short outline of a reproducible benchmark methodology we typically use for performance SLO validation. Happy to adapt to your prompts and environment.

High-level approach
- Reproducible harness: we’ll provide a containerized harness (bench/harness: v1.3) that accepts a prompt corpus (JSONL), model config, and a load profile (RPS, concurrency, burst schedule). This runs a: warmup -> measurement -> cool-down sequence and emits detailed traces + histograms.
- Measurement definitions:
  * First-token latency: time from request accepted by runtime to first token emitted (important for streaming UX).
  * End-to-end generation latency: time until final token emitted / stream closed.
  * Chunk latency: for streaming, per-chunk latency and inter-chunk jitter (stddev).
  * Token throughput: tokens/sec aggregated by model variant and batch size.
  * Tail metrics: p50/p95/p99 for both first-token and end-to-end.
  * Repro runs: run >=3 independent trials, median reported; raw histograms retained for inspection.

Bench parameters (default we recommend)
- Hardware: single-node NVIDIA A100 80GB (or equivalent). We’ll document CPU/RAM and kernel/runtime versions.
- Models: test on representative variants — e.g., Llama2-13B (fp16), Llama2-70B (int8 quantized) and any custom fine-tuned checkpoints you plan to use.
- Sequence length: run for 64, 400, and 1024 token distributions to match your short/mid/long categories.
- Batch sizing: sweep (1, 2, 4, 8) for latency-sensitive profiles; concurrency-driven batching for throughput profiles.
- Concurrency profiles: steady-state (75 QPS), burst schedule (200 QPS for 90s every 10m), and a ramp test (0->peak over 5 minutes).
- Warmup: 120s at target RPS, measurement window 300s.

Reproducibility & artifacts we will deliver
- Harness repo + pinned commit SHA and Docker image tag.
- Prompt corpus (we ask you to provide your prompt JSONL; we’ll run with it under NDA if needed).
- Raw logs: latency histograms, per-request traces (trace IDs), kernel logs, and GPU utilization traces.
- Analysis notebook: Jupyter notebook with aggregated plots and a short writeup of findings and recommended tuning (batch sizes, quantization, routing).

Streaming specifics
- We’ll measure first-chunk latency and inter-chunk intervals using instrumented client (nghttp/httptools) and provide a timeline view. For chunk-size, we usually test 32/64/128 token chunking to show tradeoffs between latency and throughput.

Security & data handling
- If you prefer, we can run the benchmark in your Dedicated environment (on-prem/VPC) so raw prompts never leave your network; otherwise we can operate under a mutual NDA and redact any sensitive tokens.

Links / artifacts (draft)
- Harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench-harness (we’ll share a pinned commit in deliverables)
- Draft benchmark plan (attached): redwood_benchmark_plan.md

If that looks good I can prepare a runnable image and a short checklist so we can kick off as soon as we have the prompt corpus and access details.

—Marcus
